name: M4RI (dense GF(2) linear algebra: Method of the Four Russians, Strassen-Winograd, PLE elimination)
baseline: Magma (proprietary computer algebra system; its asymptotically fast GF(2) matrix multiplication and elimination). None of the listed baselines (OpenBLAS, Intel MKL, Eigen, BLIS) apply because they do not operate on bit-packed GF(2) matrices.
workload: Wall-clock time of dense GF(2) matrix multiplication for square 10,000 and 16,384 dimensions, M4RI-20080821 (M4RM plus Strassen-Winograd) versus Magma, as tabulated in the Albrecht-Bard-Hart multiplication paper (arXiv 0811.1714) according to a search-engine summary; the PLE elimination paper (arXiv 1111.6549) is described in the README abstract as a gain over 'the previously fastest implementation'.
claimed_speedup: SNIPPET ONLY (search-engine summary of the tables in arXiv 0811.1714; the paper itself was not opened). 64-bit 2.33 GHz Core 2 Duo: n=10,000 Magma 2.210 s vs M4RI 1.504 s; n=16,384 Magma 8.670 s vs M4RI 6.074 s (ratios about 1.47x and 1.43x, derived from snippet data). 64-bit 2.6 GHz Opteron: n=10,000 Magma 2.656 s vs M4RI 2.490 s (about 1.07x); n=16,384 Magma 10.260 s vs M4RI 10.490 s (M4RI about 2% slower). The README (opened) quotes only 'considerable performance gains in practice when compared to the previously fastest implementation' for PLE elimination, with no numbers.
compiler_and_flags: Per the search snippet only: GCC 4.3.1 with -O2 on the Opteron and -O2 -msse2 on the Core 2 Duo (not verified). Magma version and its flags were not seen.
hardware: Per the search snippet only: 64-bit 2.33 GHz Core 2 Duo and 64-bit 2.6 GHz Opteron (2008-era machines).
stars_or_usage: 98 stars, 35 forks; adopted into SageMath and packaged for Debian, Fedora and Homebrew according to the README and its history
tradeoffs: C library for GF(2) only (GF(2^e) is the separate M4RIE library). Uses x86 SSE2 where available and optional OpenMP parallelism (--enable-openmp, described as preliminary); Linux is the supported platform, Windows and macOS are best effort. GPL-2.0-or-later is copyleft. Algorithms: M4RM and Strassen-Winograd multiplication at O(n^log2(7)), PLE factorisation, and M4RI row echelon / inversion at O(n^3/log n).
caveats: I could not open any page containing the numbers: the Bitbucket wiki 'Performance' and 'Further Reading' pages now return HTTP 404 (the Bitbucket repo is a mirror and its API lists has_wiki true, but the wiki pages are gone), and malb.bitbucket.io, martinralbrecht.wordpress.com and arXiv were blocked by the egress proxy. The numbers above come from one WebSearch result summary and are UNVERIFIED. They are 2008 numbers on 2008 hardware; M4RI is slower than Magma on the Opteron at n=16,384 and only about 1.07x faster at n=10,000, so the win is CPU-specific. The README history (2008/06/13) admits that an earlier Magma comparison on the Core 2 Duo was 'strongly biased' because a Magma build optimised for AMD64 was used on Intel64, and was corrected afterwards. Magma is proprietary, so the comparison cannot be reproduced by third parties. The repo has a bench/ directory (bench_multiplication.c, bench_elimination.c, bench_ple.c, bench_trsm.c and others) but no stored results and no comparison against any other library. From memory (not verified here) the multiplication paper appeared in ACM TOMS as Algorithm 898 (2010), which would make it peer reviewed; a verifier who can open the arXiv papers should confirm the numbers, the Magma version and the CPU, and could raise this to B.

name: COSTA (communication-optimal distributed matrix redistribution and transpose; ScaLAPACK pxgemr2d/pxtran replacement)
baseline: Intel MKL ScaLAPACK v19.1 pdgemr2d (matrix redistribution between block-cyclic layouts)
workload: pdgemr2d redistribution of square double-precision matrices with n = 20000 to 100000 between block-cyclic layouts, once with identical layouts (128x128 blocks) and once with different block sizes (36x36 to 128x128), on 8 Piz Daint nodes of 36 cores each with 16 MPI ranks (4x4 grid); COSTA run without rank relabelling and without memory pools.
claimed_speedup: README chart data labels (docs/costa-same.svg and docs/costa-diff.svg, rendered locally; time in ms, COSTA vs MKL). Same layout: n=20000 14 vs 292; 40000 56 vs 1100; 60000 128 vs 2487; 80000 208 vs 4402; 100000 324 vs 6702 (chart caption '~20x faster'; ratios 19.4x to 21.2x derived from page data). Different layouts: n=20000 188 vs 406; 40000 702 vs 1987; 60000 1608 vs 4579; 80000 2900 vs 8012; 100000 4557 vs 12737 (chart caption 'up to 3x faster'; ratios 2.2x to 2.9x derived from page data). README overview text also says it 'outperforms other scalapack implementations by orders of magnitude in some cases'.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the benchmark. CMakeLists.txt adds -funroll-loops (or -Munroll) and a build_type.cmake default that was not read; MKL ScaLAPACK v19.1 is named as the baseline; the MPI implementation and compiler are not given.
hardware: Piz Daint (Cray XC40, CSCS), 8 nodes x 36 cores, 16 MPI ranks as a 4x4 grid; the CPU model is not stated on the page.
stars_or_usage: 14 stars, 8 forks; used by COSMA, which is used by CP2K (README)
tradeoffs: Needs MPI 3 and OpenMP and CMake 3.12 or newer. Drop-in ScaLAPACK wrappers (pdgemr2d, pstran, pdtran, pctranu/c and complex variants) take effect when COSTA is linked before ScaLAPACK. Handles arbitrary irregular layouts, not only block-cyclic, and can transform several layouts in one communication round at the cost of larger messages and more memory. Optional rank relabelling can remove communication entirely when layouts differ only by a rank permutation (not used in these charts).
caveats: The baseline is MKL's ScaLAPACK redistribution routine, not a BLAS or LAPACK kernel, so it only loosely fits the blas-lapack baselines. The identical-layout case (about 20x) most likely reflects MKL's slow generic path when no data needs to move (my inference, not stated by the authors). The charts are first-party; the number of repetitions, whether times are mean or minimum, and the MKL and MPI settings are not stated (the miniapp default is n_rep=2). The README says the benchmark code is public (miniapps/pxgemr2d_miniapp.cpp, pxtran_miniapp.cpp) but the compiler, flags and CPU model are missing, so not tier A. The peer-reviewed paper (Kabic, Pintarelli, Kozhevnikov, VandeVondele, ISC 2021, Springer; arXiv 2106.06601) is cited in the README but was not opened (Springer and arXiv are blocked in this session), so I kept tier C; a verifier who can open it should consider B and check whether the paper's numbers match the README charts. 'Orders of magnitude' in the README is not shown by these charts (largest ratio about 21x). The numbers were read from the data labels of the SVG charts, which are part of the README page.

name: TTM / TLIB(TTM) (in-place tensor-times-matrix via loops-over-GEMM)
baseline: Eigen (Tensor module) and LibTorch tensor-matrix products, plus Intel MKL batched GEMM; the paper reports parity with TBLIS
workload: Mode-q tensor-times-matrix product on dense tensors of many shapes and orders, large tensor slices highlighted, as reported in the author's Journal of Computational Science 2025 paper (details not seen).
claimed_speedup: SNIPPET ONLY (search-engine summary of the paper abstract; the paper was not opened): best-performing algorithm reaches a median 2.47 TFLOPS on an Intel Xeon Gold 5318Y and 2.93 TFLOPS on an AMD EPYC 9354 for large tensor slices; 'outperforms batched GEMM implementation of Intel MKL by a factor of 2.57 with large tensor slices'; 'on average at least 6.21% and up to 334.31% faster' than frameworks implementing state-of-the-art approaches including Libtorch and Eigen; 'on par with TBLIS' for the majority of tensor shapes. The repo README gives no numbers ('For large tensors reaches peak matrix-times-matrix performance').
compiler_and_flags: Paper build not seen. Repo example/Makefile: g++ -Wall -O3 -std=c++17 -fopenmp with the BLAS chosen through BLAS_FLAG (OPENBLAS, MKL or BLIS makefile fragments).
hardware: Per the search snippet only: Intel Xeon Gold 5318Y and AMD EPYC 9354.
stars_or_usage: 5 stars, 1 fork; Python bindings (ttmpy) in repo; the README asks users to cite the Journal of Computational Science 2025 article (vol. 87, art. 102568)
tradeoffs: Header-only C++17 but requires an external BLAS (BLIS, MKL or OpenBLAS makefile fragments provided), so performance follows the chosen BLAS. float and double only, contiguously stored tensors, OpenMP 4.5 or newer for threading. In-place: no tensor transposition and no extra memory. Runtime choice of contraction mode, tensor order, extents and any linear layout. Task-loop parallelism added in late 2024.
caveats: I could not open the evidence: tore.tuhh.de returned EGRESS_BLOCKED and ScienceDirect, arXiv and ICCS pages are listed as blocked, so every number above is from one WebSearch result summary and is UNVERIFIED. Tier B rests on peer review (the README cites the paper as the article to cite) and on the snippet; it is the author's own benchmark of his own library, with the low end of the claimed range (6.21% average) marginal and TBLIS a tie. Whether the baselines were built with comparable flags, the compiler used, and whether the benchmark code is public are unknown. The repo has no baseline comparison: example/measure.cpp (g++ -O3, 10 iterations, 32 MB cache flush between runs) times only TTM's own parallel/slicing/fusion variants, and the wiki has no performance page (three of four wiki pages failed to load). The README badge says GPL while LICENSE.txt is the GNU LGPL version 3 (GitHub also shows LGPL-3.0). A verifier able to open the paper should confirm numbers, CPUs and flags and check for a public artifact repo, which could move this to A.

name: GEMM_AVX512F (wjc404; AVX-512F SGEMM/DGEMM)
workload: Single-thread SGEMM and DGEMM; matrix sizes, MKL version and the machine are not stated.
claimed_speedup: README: 'able to reach 99% MKL 1-thread performance after tuning', i.e. about 0.99x of MKL, which is parity and not a win. No GFLOPS, sizes or multi-thread numbers anywhere in the repo.
compiler_and_flags: Makefile: gcc -fopenmp --shared -fPIC -mavx512f -O2 (hand-written assembly kernel src/kernel/gemm_kernel.S plus C driver); the build used for the 99% claim is not stated.
hardware: dgemm_tune.h and sgemm_tune.h say 'parameters tuned on Xeon Platinum 8269CY'; the README does not say the 99% figure was measured on it.
stars_or_usage: 15 stars, 1 fork; sibling of the already-listed wjc404 GEMM_AVX2_FMA3
tradeoffs: Needs AVX-512F (Skylake-X / Cascade Lake class and newer Intel, some AMD). Built as DGEMM.so and SGEMM.so shared objects with an OpenMP driver whose blocking constants are hand-tuned in sgemm_tune.h and dgemm_tune.h (README: 'Please edit'). The OpenBLAS-like_implementation/ directory holds OpenBLAS-style Skylake-X kernels (dgemm 16x2 and 4x8, cgemm3m, zgemm3m, a dtrsm 16x4 solver). GPL-3.0 copyleft.
caveats: The only claim is parity (99% of MKL one-thread after tuning), written by the author with no numbers, sizes, MKL version or CPU. No benchmark program or result file exists: the repo root, src/ and OpenBLAS-like_implementation/ listings show none, and AVX512_CPUTEST.c only measures peak per-core FMA throughput, not GEMM. There is no OpenBLAS comparison even though the code comments say parts are 'similar to' OpenBLAS routines. Last commit 2022-05-22 (default branch develop), so the code predates newer MKL and OpenBLAS SkylakeX kernels. Kept as a low-confidence record because it is not faster than the baseline.

name: fast_matmul (NinjadenMu; didactic BLIS-style SGEMM for Apple M4)
baseline: OpenBLAS as called through NumPy (float32 A @ B in scripts/openblas.py)
workload: Square float32 matrix multiplication for n = 100, 200, 300, ... each run once until a cumulative 5 s budget is used (scripts/driver.py), custom BLIS-style code versus NumPy with OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 and with default threads.
claimed_speedup: README text: the single-threaded BLIS-style implementation is 'comparable to an OpenBLAS build targeting Apple Silicon (with the difference being too small for me to reliably measure)' and the multi-threaded one is 'noticeably faster (probably due to better load balancing on my particular M4 spec)'; '~200x faster (40x with just one thread)' is against the project's own naive loop, not OpenBLAS. Read by eye from plots/plot.png: single-threaded OpenBLAS reaches n=3100 at about 4.55 s cumulative versus BLIS-style n=3000 at about 4.08 s (curves overlap); multi-threaded BLIS-style reaches n=4500 at about 4.08 s versus multi-threaded OpenBLAS n=4200 at about 4.7 s.
compiler_and_flags: Makefile: clang -O3 -ffast-math -march=native (commented alternative -mcpu=apple-m4), OpenMP via Homebrew libomp, -fno-vectorize on the early didactic versions. The clang version is not stated and neither are the NumPy or OpenBLAS versions.
hardware: Apple M4 (README: 'my Apple M4'); core configuration and RAM not stated.
stars_or_usage: 0 stars, 0 forks; same author as MuBLIS (which is already on the known list)
tradeoffs: Teaching code: float32 only, square matrices only, column-major, no transposes or alpha/beta and no BLAS interface. ARM NEON intrinsics (Apple Silicon only; the README says x86 needs retuned block sizes and AVX kernels). Fixed 12x8 register tile, cache block sizes tuned by scripts/tuner.py, OpenMP dynamic scheduling for the parallel version. No LICENSE file, so the code cannot be copied.
caveats: The benchmark treats the two sides unequally. The custom side runs ./bench with one untimed warm-up call and one timed call into a pre-zeroed output buffer (utils/bench.c). The baseline times a single NumPy A @ B call inside Python with no warm-up and with the result matrix allocated inside the timed region. There is one measurement per n, no repeats or variance, the metric is 'largest n within a cumulative time budget' rather than GFLOPS, and the custom code is built with -ffast-math. The README does not record whether NumPy used OpenBLAS or Accelerate on the M4. Parity is the only single-thread result, and the author himself attributes the multi-thread gap to load balancing on his particular M4, which may be a P/E-core scheduling artifact. Numbers are read by eye from the plot image. By the literal tier-A rule (public script, clang flags, Apple M4) this would be A, but I held it at C because of the asymmetric method; a verifier may revisit. The author's deep-dive post on ninjadenmu.github.io is egress-blocked. No license.

name: libMetalFloat64 (philipturner/metal-float64; emulated FP64 on Apple GPUs)
baseline: Native hardware FP64 on the Apple Silicon CPU (NEON) in the README table, and OpenCL FP64 in the precision table; the listed baselines GMP and MPFR are not compared
workload: Theoretical maximum scalar giga-operations per second per operation (FFMA, FADD, FMUL, FCMPSEL, FCMP, FRECIP, FDIV, FRSQRT, FSQRT) for a reference system with an 8-core 3.064 GHz ARM CPU (four 128-bit vector ALUs per core) and a 32-core 1.296 GHz Apple GPU, computed from instruction counts and not measured.
claimed_speedup: README table of theoretical Gops, CPU FP64 vs GPU FP32x2 (double-single) emulation: FFMA 392 vs 590, FADD 196 vs 482, FMUL 196 vs 758, FCMPSEL 196 vs 2123, FCMP 196 vs 1769, FRECIP 49 vs 196, FDIV 49 vs 183, FRSQRT 49 vs 171, FSQRT 49 vs 189 (ratios 1.5x to 10.8x, derived from page data). The 'GPU eFP64' column, the IEEE-compliant mode, is empty. Text: additions and multiplications 'will have 1/32-1/64 the throughput of their 32-bit counterparts', an estimate.
hardware: README reference system: 8-core 3.064 GHz ARM CPU and 32-core 1.296 GHz Apple GPU; the chip is not named.
tradeoffs: Swift package that builds a Metal dynamic library and headers; needs an Apple6-family or newer GPU (A13 and later, Metal 3) and macOS Ventura on Intel Macs. Two precisions: float64_t is IEEE-compliant but the README gives no throughput for it, while float32x2_t has 1+47 mantissa bits, flushes denormals and has undefined INF/NaN results. Larger functions are called through the dynamic library, so inlining is partial. The planned 64-bit atomics use a lock buffer and the README warns that a missing useResource call can freeze half the GPU. Matrix types, division, square root and transcendentals were still planned; the README states the library is 'not a finished library'.
caveats: The README says 'Still in the planning stage - this is not a finished library!'. There is no measured benchmark anywhere I could open: the table is labelled 'maximum theoretical performance', the eFP64 (IEEE) column is blank and the precision table is mostly '???'. The related philipturner/openmm-benchmarks FP64Emulation folder holds only Trial1.swift, Trial2.swift, Trial3.cl and a chat transcript, and I found no timing numbers in the trial files. The comparison is against the CPU's hardware double, not against the category baselines GMP or MPFR (software arbitrary precision), so it does not fit this category; it is filed here because the assignment placed it there. I set tier D because no real workload was timed; the README does contain theoretical numbers, so a verifier could treat it as C. Abandoned and archived.
